You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

Blues – A First Step Toward Improvisation
No matter the style, everyone starts learning the blues to get into the world of
improvisation. The reason for this is because the blues basically has one scale (the blues
scale). It can be applied over all the chords in the blues form, including all the cadences and
turnarrounds. Later on we will learn how to use this scale over many types of songs.


The Blues Scale
The blues scale is a minor pentatonic scale with an added note. This note is called a "blue"
note. Normally we use this scale from the key we are in rather than over an individual
chord. Because it can be used over all the blues chords at once, this simpliBies playing over
all the chord changes. Be careful not to rely on this technique. It will make you sound like a
"lazy" improviser. Your lines will lack variation and will sound stagnant.

Because of the connection between the blues scale and the minor pentatonic scale we can
consider that there is a major blues scale, that actually will be the same scale, but
starting from the 3rd degree of the original blues scale (now minor blues scale). See below:

  Minor Blues Scale
  The minor blues scale should be used over the major or minor tonality, summarizing all the

  The major blues scale can be played over any individual major chord, including the major

  Improvisation is something that goes beyond our harmony knowledge and rhythmic concepts.
  First we must understand "when and how" this information is to be used to improve our solos. To
  make this clear, we will learn three ways to move our improvisation over song forms, and we will
  call this: improvisation positioning.



  1) Playing Early Notes:

  Improvise by playing early notes means to anticipate the melodies in anticipation of the chord,
  before the chord arrives. This is the most difficult positioning to master.



  2) Playing on the Head:

  Improvise by playing on the head means to follow the exact harmonies of the tune.



  3) Playing Late Notes:

  Improvise by playing late notes means to play after the chord changes. This is the easiest and
  simplest way.

  There are two different ways to use these three concepts above:



  a) You can play one scale, and what will be important is how you move rhythmically over the
  song. When we play a blues for example, we can use a simple pentatonic scale over the whole
  sequence of chords, we do not have to be concerned about which scales to use, only with
  positioning the melodies, even if they are simple.


  b) You can use these positioning concepts playing many scales but moving and following the
  harmony exactly. In other words, you change the scale when the harmony changes.
